Bush Beans Grow, Flower, and Begin Fruit Production in Washed LHS-1 
Supplemented With Less Than 10% Organic Matter 
 
 
 
Plant The Moon Challenge Spring 2023 
 
 
 
Team #: 
 
 
13135 
Team Name: 
 
The Williams Family 
Team Coach: 
 
Kathryn Williams 
Challenge: 
 
 
Plant the Moon 
Challenge Division: 
Professional 
Location: 
 
 
Our Family Home, St. Louis, Missouri, USA 
 
 
Primary Investigators: 
Kathryn M. Williams (Stay-At-Home-Parent, PhD in Evolution) 
and William C. Reed (Grandfather, Retired Electrical Engineer) 
 
Research Assistants: 
Sebastian Williams (Age 9) and Alexander Williams (Age 9) 
 
 
ABSTRACT 
 
 
Returning to the Moon and undertaking long-duration human exploration on the Moon 
are primary goals of NASA’s Artemis Program. To sustain extended human exploration on the 
Moon, we must learn to grow crops using in situ resources. Some crops have already been grown 
in lunar regolith simulants, but more research is needed to determine the most efficient way to 
produce plants in such a harsh environment. Growing crops in lunar regolith simulants, such as 
LHS-1, requires overcoming multiple chemical and physical challenges, including the absence of 
essential elements like Nitrogen, Sulfur and Chlorine, toxic concentrations of elements such as 
Calcium, very high pH, and poor drainage qualities. Many prior studies have sought to overcome 
these challenges by using large quantities of organic matter (50%), which does not directly 
address the toxicity caused by high calcium. To expand our knowledge of growing crops on the 
Moon, we chose to study Bush Bean growth in LHS-1. Through our research, we aimed (1) to 
grow Bush Bean plants that produced fruit, (2) use less organic matter and amendments than 
previous research, and (3) demonstrate the efficacy of in situ resources, such as biosolids, on 
crop production. Two innovative features of our approach are (1) washing LHS-1 with distilled 
water to reduce toxic concentrations of Ca before using it as a growth substrate, and (2) the 
design and implementation of a Soil Atmosphere Circulation System to enhance drainage and 
maintain the soil atmosphere. We show that Bush Beans can germinate, grow, flower, and begin 
to produce fruit in LHS-1 amended with less than 10% organic matter after 44 days of growth. 
We believe this growth reflects the value of washing the LHS-1 prior to using it as a growth 
substrate and of maintaining the soil atmosphere.

2 
INTRODUCTION 
 
 
Returning to the Moon and establishing a human presence on the Moon is a primary goal 
of NASA’s Artemis program. Essential to any long-duration human presence on the Moon is a 
reliable food source. It currently costs approximately $100,000 to send each pound of material to 
and from the Moon (Jones 2022). Given that cost, it is imperative to limit the amount of material 
sent between the Moon and Earth. In May 2022, Paul et al. (2022) grew the model plant 
Arabidopsis thaliana in lunar regolith obtained from the Apollo missions to the Moon, 
demonstrating the potential for growing crops via in situ resource utilization (ISRU). 
Multiple crops have already been grown in lunar regolith simulant. Previous studies have 
grown tomato, cress, radish, rye, rocket, quinoa, and peas (Wamelink et al. 2019, Wamelink et 
al. 2014). Consistent with the growth experiments in actual lunar regolith (Paul et al. 2022), 
plants grown in lunar regolith simulant tend to exhibit reduced growth, flowering and fruiting 
compared to controls. The ability to grow crops on the Moon in sufficient varieties and quantities 
to support human health remains largely unknown. Much more research is needed for crop 
production on the Moon via ISRU to become a reality. 
 
Growing crops successfully in lunar regolith simulant presents multiple challenges 
related to its chemical and physical composition. Chemically, lunar regolith simulants, such as 
LHS-1, contain insufficient amounts of some elements and excessive quantities of other elements 
for crops. Plant growth requires at least 16 essential elements obtained from soil (Taiz & Zeiger 
2002). Some of these elements, including Nitrogen (N), Sulfur (S), and Chlorine (Cl), are 
completely absent from LHS-1 (Exolith Labs, 2022). Conversely, elements such as Calcium (Ca) 
are present in detrimental amounts. LHS-1 contains 9.36% Ca in the form of calcium oxide 
(Exolith Labs, 2022), which is more than 4X the Ca needs for most plants (Kelling & Schulte 
2004, Broadly et al. 2003). Excess Ca leads to toxicity by increasing pH and inhibiting nutrient 
uptake by plants (White & Broadly, 2003). LHS-1 also contains sodium (Na) in the form of 
Na2O, which can contribute to salt stress (Doungous et al. 2022; Shi et al. 2017). Physically, 
LHS-1 contains particulates that are prone to forming agglutinates. These agglutinates decrease 
the movement of water and gases in the soil atmosphere, which can inhibit plant growth. 
Collectively, the chemical and physical properties of LHS-1 make using it as a primary substrate 
for growing crops a formidable challenge. 
 
Most recent attempts to grow crops in LHS-1 have relied on large quantities of organic 
matter (50%), including peat moss, Earth soil, sawdust, worm castings, and compost, as well as 
fertilizers such as Miracle Grow, ammonium sulfate, urine, and biosolids (PTMC Spring 2021 – 
Fall 2022). The primary impact of these amendments is to increase nutrient concentration in 
LHS-1 and improve soil tilth. However, nutrient uptake by plants also depends on the pH of the 
substrate. LHS-1 has a pH of 8 – 9, which is far too alkaline for most crops to adequately uptake 
nutrients, even if they are available. Large quantities of organic matter can alter the pH of 
substrates containing LHS-1, but even a 50:50 mix of LHS-1 to organic matter will not eliminate 
toxicity caused by Ca. If most crops grow best with approximately 2% Ca, then the Ca content of 
LHS-1 will need to be reduced by at least 75%. To mitigate discrepancies between the growth 
requirements of plants and the inherent properties of LHS-1, successful crop production requires 
the addition of multiple nutrients, development of the soil atmosphere, and reduction of 
inhibitory chemical concentrations. 
 
To advance our knowledge of crop production on the Moon, we chose to participate in 
the Plant The Moon Challenge and study Bush Bean growth in LHS-1. We chose Bush Beans

3 
because according to the Old Farmer’s Almanac, a trusted source for gardening advice since 
1792, they are “easy to grow—even in limited space—and incredibly productive!” (Old Farmer’s 
Almanac, 2023). Also, Bush Beans are nutritionally beneficial for humans, self-pollinating, and 
we have previous experience growing this crop successfully in our home garden. The guiding 
principle we used to tackle this challenge was that matter cannot be created nor destroyed. We 
believe that ISRU on the Moon should be maximized and the amount of materials transported 
from Earth to the Moon should be minimized. Our objectives for the PTMC Spring 2023 were 
(1) to grow Bush Bean plants that produced fruit in LHS-1, (2) use less organic matter and 
amendments than previous research, and (3) demonstrate the efficacy of in situ resources, such as 
biosolids, on crop production. 
 
In this study, we show that Bush Beans can germinate, grow, flower, and begin to 
produce fruit in LHS-1 amended with less than 10% organic matter (Figure 1). Two innovative 
features of our approach are (1) washing LHS-1 with distilled water to reduce Ca before using it 
as a growth substrate, and (2) the design and implementation of a Soil Atmosphere Circulation 
System to enhance drainage and maintain the soil atmosphere. We had two hypotheses: (1) 
Washing LHS-1 with distilled water would reduce its Ca content, and (2) that the more biosolids 
added to a growth substrate, the greater the plant growth and crop yield. To test our first 
hypotheses, we assessed the pH of LHS-1 before and after washing. The pH of LHS-1 went from 
8 – 9 down to 7 – 8 after washing, which is consistent with a reduction in Ca. To test our second 
hypothesis, we observed the growth of green beans in LHS-1 supplemented with 0, 3.5, 7, 10.5, 
and 14 grams (g) of biosolids. Growth varied across pots but did not correlate with the amount of 
biosolids. The major finding of our study was the flowering a fruit formation of Bush Beans 
grown in LHS-1 supplemented with less than 10% organic matter. All our Bush Bean plants 
were still alive at 46 days of growth. We believe this growth reflects the value of washing the 
LHS-1 prior to using it as a growth substrate and of maintaining the soil atmosphere.

4 
Figure 1. Bush Beans can flower and produce fruit in LHS-1 amended with less than 10% 
organic matter. Bush bean plants grown in LHS-1 (A, C) or Topsoil (B, D), without biosolids 
(Top Row) or with 14 g biosolids (Bottom Row) after 46 days. Plants grown in LHS-1 survive to 
produce flowers (A and B) and fruits (only A). However, they are much small and less 
productive than plants grown in Topsoil (C and D). Plants grown in both LHS-1 and Topsoil 
exhibited some chlorosis. However, only plants grown in LHS-1 exhibited senescence.

METHODS 
 
Novel Lunar Regolith Wash Method 
 
LHS-1 contains 9.36% calcium (Ca), which is more the 4X the amount recommended for 
growing Bush Beans (Kelling & Schulte (2004)). For plants to grow well, this toxic 
concentration of Ca must be reduced. Given that Ca is soluble in water, we reasoned that we 
could remove excess Ca from LHS-1 by first washing it with copious amounts of water. To 
remove Ca from LHS-1, we mixed 5 kg of dry LHS-1 containing 468 g of Ca with 16 L of 
distilled water. We then used a ladle to remove 12 L of the resulting solution, or an etimated 351 
g of Ca. Assuming the calcium dissolved readily in the distilled water, the remaining regolith 
contained approximately 114 g, or about 2%, Ca. During this process, we also removed other 
water-soluble elements, including Sodium (Na), Potassium (K), and Magnesium (Mg), as well as 
clay particles that were held in suspension. 
After this wash process, the LHS-1 resembled very wet mud with far too much water for 
planting. To remove most of the remaining water, we heated the LHS-1 on a camp stove and 
allowed the water to evaporate into the outdoor air. Due to challenges we encountered attempting 
this novel approach in a home setting, e.g., all of the containers we used were thrifted from 
Goodwill and one of them broke during heating, a small amount of LHS-1 was lost. After 
washing and evaporating most of the remaining water, we ended up with 5,210 g of LHS-1 with 
19% water content (approximately 4,220 g dry weight). 
 
Amendments and Fertilizer 
LHS-1 lacks multiple elements essential for plant growth, including N, S, and Cl. 
Additionally, the washing treatment we used to remove excess Ca, likely also removed other 
water-soluble elements essential for plant growth, including K and Mg. While many prior studies 
have amended LHS-1 with 50% organic matter to alleviate some of these nutritional deficiencies, 
reduce pH, and improve soil tilth (PTMC Spring 2021 – Fall 2022), one of our objectives was to 
reduce the amount of organic matter added to the LHS-1 via ISRU. 
To determine the amount of organic matter that could potentially be available in situ on 
the Moon, we developed the Three Season Compost Model (Figure 2). Based on this model, we 
used 18 g of organic matter representing three prior growing seasons in each pot. Since Spring 
2023 is our first time participating in the PTMC Challenge, we did not have any organic matter 
from prior growing seasons. To mimic organic matter from three prior growing seasons, we used 
Timothy Hay for minus 1 season, Composted Leaves for minus 2 seasons, and Peat Moss for 
minus 3 seasons. These materials represent organic matter in various stages of decay and would 
ideally be acquired from crops grown entirely on the Moon.

6 
FIGURE 2. Three Season Compost Model. In this model we assume each plant possesses 30 g 
of organic matter and that 40% of this organic matter comprise fruit that will be consumed by 
space explorers or used for seeds. The remaining 60% of organic matter comprises roots and 
shoots that can be composted. In this model each plant yields 18 g of compostable material per 
season. Given that this is our first season in the PTMC, we chose three different types of organic 
matter to represent compost from three prior seasons, including Timothy Hay (minus 1 season), 
Composted Leaves (minus 2 seasons), and Peat Moss (minus 3 seasons). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Although amending LHS-1 with organic matter from 3 prior growing seasons will 
provide some nutrients and improve soil tilth, it will not provide sufficient nutrition for robust 
plant growth and food production. First, nutrients lost from human consumption of fruit must 
also be replaced. To estimate the amount of biosolids that could be reclaimed as fertilizer on the 
Moon, we developed a Biosolid Reclamation Model (Figure 3). Using this model, we estimated 
that the maximum amount of biosolids that could be obtained in situ was 14 g per plant per 
growing season. We wanted to observe whether different amounts of biosolids impacted plant 
growth, so each pot received 0, 3.5, 7, 10.5, or 14 g of biosolids (sourced from St. Joseph, 
Missouri Water Protection Agency).

Even with the addition of organic matter representing and biosolids, more fertilization 
was necessary to compensate for nutrients lost to seed production and to account for other known 
deficiencies in LHS-1. Additional amendments and fertilizers added to each pot included: 21 g 
Kelp Meal (Neptune’s Harvest Kelp Meal, Ocean Crest Seafoods, Gloucester, MA), 0.17 g of 
21% Ammonium Sulfate (Hi-Yield) , 0.13 g of 18% Super Phosphate (Hi-Yield), and 0.09 g of 
60% Potash (Hi-Yield). Kelp meal contains Cl, which is essential for plant growth, as well as 
cobalt, which facilitates nodule formation and nitrogen-fixation by bacteria in symbiotic 
relationship with legumes such as Bush Beans. The total amount of organic matter, including 
Timothy Hay, Composted Leaves, Peat Moss and Kelp Meal, added to each pot was 75 g, or 
8.8% for the pots with LHS-1 and 7.5% for the pots with Topsoil (LHS-1 pots received a 
somewhat greater fraction of organic matter because some LHS-1 was lots during the wash 
treatment). Ammonium Sulfate, Super Phosphate, and Potash were applied to pots at planting 
time and after the development of first true leaves according to recommendations by the 
University of Wisconsin Extension. For an overview of the additions and subtractions we made 
to the LHS-1 before plants, see Table 1.

Midway through the growth experiment most plants in both LHS-1 and Topsoil began 
exhibiting signs of chlorosis. We suspect this stress was caused by our watering method in the 
first portion of our experiment. To help mitigate this problem, we applied two doses of chelated 
liquid iron applied according to manufacturer instructions (ferti-lome Chelated Liquid Iron and 
Other Micronutrients, Bonham, TX). 
 
Seeds and Planting 
 
Blue Lake 274 Bush Beans were grown in either 844 g of LHS-1 or 1,000 g of Topsoil in 
8-inch round plastic pots amended with 75 g of organic matter plus fertilizer as described above. 
We had initially intended to use equal amount of LHS-1 and Topsoil. However, a small amount 
of LHS-1 was lost during the washing process (see above) and all other components had already 
been measured and mixed by that time. The total amount of organic matter used in each pot was 
8.8% for the pots with LHS-1 and 7.5% for the pots with Topsoil. 
Each pot was sown with three seeds approximately 1 inch below the surface of the soil. 
Seeds were sprinkled with ¼ teaspoon of granular Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Nature’s Aid 1x108 
viable cells per g of Bradyrhizobium sp., Rhizobium leguminosarum and R. phaseoli). Following 
germination, seeds were thinned to 1 plant per pot. 
 
Novel Soil Atmosphere Circulation System 
The physical properties of LHS-1 inhibit the flow of water away from plant roots. 
Additionally, low gravity on the Moon will exacerbate the poor drainage qualities of lunar 
regolith. Without sufficient drainage, growth substrates become waterlogged, reducing gas 
exchange between roots and the soil atmosphere. To grow crops on the Moon, terraforming 
endeavors must ensure (1) adequate water drainage, (2) soil surface air flow, and (3) subsurface 
air flow. In the absences of these elements, plants cannot thrive. 
For our experiment, we engineered a Soil Atmosphere Circulation System comprised of 
(1) our Low Gravity Drainage Enhancement System (LGDES), (2) an 18-inch diameter pedestal 
fan, and (3) our Subsurface Atmosphere Ventilation System (Figure 4). First, to facilitate 
adequate water drainage in LHS-1 and on the Moon, our LGDES was comprised of a filter, 
collection reservoir, and vacuum connected via tubing. Following watering, excess water was 
removed from each pot via suction created by 2.5 gallon 2-HP shopvac (Craftsman). Water from 
each pot was collected in a corresponding reservoir. Second, to ensure air flow on the soil 
surface, we positioned an 18-inch diameter pedestal fan (Lasko) on one side of the grow room, 
12 inches above the soil surface. Third, to promote subsurface air flow, we installed our Soil 
Atmosphere Ventilation System (SAVS). The SAVS consists of a 4” square, 12 volt computer 
fan (Wathai), bespoke pressure collator, and tubing that connects each collection reservoir used 
in the LGDES to the computer fan. The objective of SAVS was to create equal and subtle air 
flow from above the soil surface, down through the soil, and away from plant roots. In our 
approach, air flow from the SAVS was vented into the grow room. The goal of our Soil 
Atmosphere Circulation System was to overcome the poor drainage qualities inherent to LHS-1 
and potentially identify a way to mitigate drainage problems inherent to crop production in low-
gravity environments.

Watering 
 
All pots were watered with 100 – 400 ml of distilled water every 1 to 4 days. The amount 
of water varied over the course of the experiment. Initially, we sought to keep the growth 
substrate continually moist to prompt seed germination. As roots developed, we began to allow 
the topmost surface of the soil to dry between waterings. Following each watering, we extracted 
excess water from each pot using the shopvac attached to the LGDES for 10 – 20 seconds for 
pots containing Topsoil and 20 – 30 seconds for pots containing LHS-1 (the two substrates 
exhibited different rates of water drainage). The amount of water we collected varied from 0 to 
upwards of 300 ml of water, depending on how moist the soil was prior to watering and how 
much water was added. 
Midway through the experiment we began using a combination of re-claimed water and 
distilled water. For the first part of the experiment, we combined the extracted water from each 
pot into a large storage container. Initially, we hesitated re-using this water due to concern about 
it containing dissolved sodium (Na), which is detrimental for plant growth. Following a note 
made by Dr. Robert Heinse during the March 22, 2023 Q&A Session about the loss of nutrients 
into the extracted water and apparent nutrient deficiencies beginning at around 24 days of 
growth, we opted to begin re-using water extracted during subsequent waterings. We chose not 
to re-use the extracted water we had collected and combined during the first part of the 
experiment for two reasons: (1) we did not know how many nutrients were in the solution, and 
(2) the solution had started to grow algae. Although Na in the collected water may not be ideal 
for plant growth, we agree with Dr. Heinse’s recommendation to re-use extracted water to retain 
nutrients. Regrettably, we believe we may have lost an unknown, but likely helpful amount of 
nutrients in the first part of our experiment. 
 
Lighting and Temperature 
We used a Spider Farm SF4000 LED Grow Light to expose plants to alternating 
light/dark periods ranging from approximately 14 hours 30 minutes of light to 15 hours 30 
minutes of light. The duration of the light period was increased every 7 – 10 days according to 
the daylength in Wisconsin during green bean growing season. Wisconsin produces the most 
green beans of any state in the USA, and thus represents ideal growing conditions for this crop 
plant. The intensity of the light was increased depending on the growth stage of the plants 
(germination, leaf growth and flowering), according to manufacturer recommendations. Plants 
were grown in the basement of our family home with ambient temperatures ranging from 64 to 
67°F. 
 
 
RESULTS 
 
Novel Lunar Regolith Wash Method 
 
Washing LHS-1 with distilled water decreases its pH (Figure 5). Prior to washing, the pH 
of LHS-1 was 8 – 9. To remove water soluble molecules from LHS-1, we mixed dry LHS-1 with 
copious amounts of distilled water. We then removed 75% of the resulting water with dissolved 
molecules (Moon Milk), before evaporating most of the remaining water from the LHS-1. The 
starting pH of the distilled water was 7, and the pH of the Moon Milk was 8 – 9. This difference 
in pH is consistent with the dissolution of cations from LHS-1 into the distilled water upon 
mixing. The pH of LHS-1 after washing was 7 – 8, which indicates an approximately 10-fold

12 
decrease in pH relative to unwashed LHS-1. This decrease is consistent with the removal of 
cations, such as Ca+, from LHS-1. Notably, the pH of our Topsoil control was also 7 – 8. 
 
In addition to removing soluble ions during our Lunar Regolith Wash, we also removed 
clay-like particles that remained in suspension. We estimate that we removed 112.5 g of clay-like 
particles from the 5 kg of LHS-1 we had available for our experiment. These clay-like particles 
contribute to agglutinates in LHS-1. Removing a fraction of these particles likely also reduced 
compaction the LHS-1 during plant growth. 
 
Figure 5. Novel Lunar Regolith Wash Method reduced the pH of LHS-1 from 8 – 9 to 7 – 8, 
which is the same as Topsoil. Shown in the images are (A) pH of LHS-1 before washing, (B) 
pH of distilled water, (C) pH of Moon Milk, (D) pH of LHS-1 after washing, (E) pH of LHS-1 at 
planting, and (F) pH of Topsoil at planting. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Novel Soil Atmosphere Circulation System 
 
The LGEDS effectively removes water from pots (Figure 6). After each watering, excess 
water was extracted from each pot using the LGEDS. Prior to using the system, water tended to 
pool on top of LHS-1, although it drained readily through the Topsoil. Using the LGEDS 
facilitated the movement of water through the substrate and out of the bottom of the pot. The 
amount of water collected varied from 0 – 300 ml, depending on the moisture content of the 
substrate prior and the amount of water added. The amount of time it took to remove excess 
water varied between pots with LHS-1 and Topsoil. Water was extracted more quickly from pots 
containing Topsoil (10 – 20 seconds of suction) compared to pots containing LHS-1 (20 – 30 
seconds of suction). Notably, the color of the extracted water difference between the two 
substrates as well, with the LHS-1 extracts tending to be much darker. The precise reason for this

difference remains uncertain, but it is a bit surprising since the LHS-1 is so much lighter in color 
than Topsoil. 
 
Figure 6. Low Drainage Enhancement System (LGDES) effectively removes excess water 
from pots. Show is (Top Row) LHS-1 band (Bottom Row) Topsoil before and after extracting 
and collecting excess water. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Except during watering and active use of the LGEDS, the room fan and SAVS operated 
almost continuously. It took us several days post-planting to install the room fan, and several 
more days to finish the installation of the SAVS. Although we were unable to directly measure 
the impact of these units on the soil surface and subsurface, several observations are consistent 
with their efficacy. First, prior to using the room fan we observed mold growth on the surface of 
the substrate in each pot (data not shown). Once we installed the room fan, the mold diminished, 
suggesting that the room fan helped to evaporate moisture on the substrate surface. Next, after 
installing the SAVS, air vented continuously from the computer fan and emitted a mineral-like 
smell. The substrate also seemed less prone to compaction. Together, these observations suggest 
that the Soil Atmosphere Circulation System helped to enhance air flow above and within the 
substrates.

14 
Plant Growth 
 
Seeds germinated in all pots of both LHS-1 and Topsoil. The number of days until 
germination, which we defined by the emergence of the first true leaves, was 10 to 12 days for 
LHS-1, and 9 to 16 days for Topsoil. The average number of days to germination was 11 for 
seeds sown in LHS-1 and10.3 days for seeds sown in Topsoil (data not shown). Within 12 days 
of planting, most pots had at least one seed that fully germinated. 
 
For the first 24 days of growth, the most notable difference between plants grown in 
LHS-1 and Topsoil was leaf color (Figure 7). Plants grown in LHS-1 were medium- to deep-
green while plants grown in Topsoil were yellow-green to medium-green. This color difference 
persisted until about day 22 to 25. By 25 days of growth, variation between the plants became 
more apparent. For example, by Day 25 the plant grown in LHS-1 supplemented with 3.5 g of 
biosolids had small, curled leaves that were yellow with dark pigmentation. Meanwhile, plants 
grown in LHS-1 supplemented with 0 and 14 g of biosolid remained deep-green. We suspect that 
some of this variance is due to chance, but it could also be related to variation in the rates of the 
development between the plants. In other words, faster growing plants may exhibit signs of stress 
earlier because their nutritional demands increase faster. Plants grown in Topsoil also exhibited 
signs of stress (yellowing leaves),but were more consistent in their appearance overall. 
 
Figure 7. Leaf color varied between plants grown in LHS-1 and Topsoil after 25 days of growth. 
Plants grown in LHS-1 tended to emerge medium- to dark-green, but they gradually showed 
signs of stress as they matured (yellowing, curling, dark pigmentation). Plants grown in Topsoil 
tended to emerge bright green but gradually developed chlorosis as they matured.

While we anticipated that plants grown in LHS-1 were likely show signs of stress, we 
were surprised that all the plants grown in Topsoil also showed signs of stress. In particular, the 
leaves of plants grown in Topsoil were large, but yellow with dark venation (chlorosis). This 
observation suggested a nutrient deficiency. Up until midway through the grow period we did 
not re-use water extracted via the LGDES following watering. Given that nearly all amendments 
and fertilizers were applied in the first 14 days of growth, we suspect we inadvertently extracted 
many of the nutrients we had added along with the water. To address this possibility, we decided 
to treat all plants for chlorosis with chelated liquid iron and to begin re-using water we extracted 
via the LGDES during watering. 
 
 By Day 45 all plants in both LHS-1 and Topsoil remained alive (Figure 8). Following 
the treatment with chelated liquid iron, plants in both substrates show signs of improved growth. 
Development progressed for all plants and all new leaves were medium-green rather than yellow 
(personal observations). However, as time progressed, the greening was only sustained by the 
plants grown in Topsoil. Eventually, the leaves on plants grown in LHS-1 began to senesce and 
gradually fall off the plants.

Our most notable growth result was the formation of flowers on two plants grown in 
LHS-1, and fruit on one plant grown in LHS-1 (Figure 1). Given the numerous challenges to 
growing plants in LHS-1, that this is our first attempt at ever growing plants in this substrate, and 
that we used less than 10% organic matter in our approach, we are very excited by this result! 
Compared to plants grown in LHS-1, plants grown Topsoil controls tended to be much large, and 
exhibited numerous flowers and fruits. 
 
 
CONCLUSIONS 
 
Participating in the Plant The Moon Challenge Spring 2023 has been awesome! Our 
family team, including three generations, worked together to learn about the challenges of space 
exploration and crop production in the wild environments that exist beyond our Earth. As 
participants in this challenge, we felt like trailblazers trying to find a way to grow plants in a 
totally new and different way. Lunar regolith possesses numerous challenges for plants adapted

to growing in Earth soil. The innovative contributions of our work include the washing method 
we used to prepare the lunar regolith simulant for growing plants and the design of a new 
drainage and ventilation system to maintain the soil atmosphere. As a family we overcame 
multiple challenges to advanced our knowledge, and we hope that the findings of our research 
helps pave the way for future explorers.
